questions.prompt: In an unweighted graph, which traversal finds shortest paths in number of edges from a source?
options: Breadth-first search
Depth-first search
A topological sort
Kruskal's algorithm
answer: Breadth-first search
questions.explanation: BFS explores vertices in increasing distance layers. The first discovery of a vertex therefore uses a minimum-edge path from the source.

questions.prompt: In a BFS tree rooted at s, a vertex v is at level 4. How many edges are in the shortest unweighted path from s to v?
questions.explanation: BFS level equals shortest-path distance measured in edges for an unweighted graph. Level 4 therefore corresponds to a path of four edges.

questions.prompt: Which statements about BFS are correct for an adjacency-list graph?
options: Its running time is O(V+E)
It uses a queue
It can compute unweighted shortest-path distances
It requires all edge weights to be equal and positive
answer: Its running time is O(V+E)
It uses a queue
It can compute unweighted shortest-path distances
questions.explanation: BFS scans each vertex and edge a constant number of times using a queue. The shortest-path guarantee applies to unweighted or equal-weight edges, including zero as a common unweighted model; positive edge weights are not required.

questions.prompt: A graph is represented by adjacency lists. What is the BFS time complexity over all vertices and edges?
options: O(V+E)
O(V²)
O(E log V)
O(VE)
answer: O(V+E)
questions.explanation: BFS initializes each vertex once and scans each adjacency-list edge once, leading to O(V+E) total time.

questions.prompt: A connected undirected graph has 12 vertices and 17 edges. How many edges does a BFS spanning tree contain?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree on 12 vertices has V−1=11 edges, independent of the number of extra graph edges.

questions.prompt: In DFS, a vertex is marked discovered when it is first entered. What is the main purpose of this mark?
options: To avoid recursively exploring the same vertex indefinitely
To sort vertices by weight
To guarantee shortest paths
To count all spanning trees
answer: To avoid recursively exploring the same vertex indefinitely
questions.explanation: Marking a vertex on discovery prevents repeated visits through cycles and ensures each vertex is processed a bounded number of times.

questions.prompt: Which statements about depth-first search are correct?
options: It can be implemented using recursion or an explicit stack
It can find connected components in an undirected graph
Its discovery/finish times support edge classification
It always finds an unweighted shortest path
answer: It can be implemented using recursion or an explicit stack
It can find connected components in an undirected graph
Its discovery/finish times support edge classification
questions.explanation: DFS explores deeply before backtracking and can be implemented recursively or iteratively. It supports connectivity and structural analyses, but unlike BFS it does not generally yield shortest paths.

questions.prompt: A DFS forest of an undirected graph has 4 connected components. How many DFS trees are in the forest?
questions.explanation: A complete DFS over an undirected graph starts a new tree once for each undiscovered connected component, yielding four trees.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has a back edge during DFS. What does this imply?
options: The graph contains a directed cycle
The graph is necessarily acyclic
The edge is a cross edge only
All vertices have the same finish time
answer: The graph contains a directed cycle
questions.explanation: A back edge points from a vertex to an ancestor in the active DFS recursion stack, forming a directed cycle with the tree path back to that ancestor.

questions.prompt: Which statements characterize a topological ordering?
options: It is a linear ordering of vertices of a DAG
For every directed edge u→v, u appears before v
Every directed graph has at least one topological ordering
A directed cycle prevents a topological ordering
answer: It is a linear ordering of vertices of a DAG
For every directed edge u→v, u appears before v
A directed cycle prevents a topological ordering
questions.explanation: A topological order respects every edge direction and exists exactly for directed acyclic graphs. A directed cycle imposes contradictory precedence constraints.

questions.prompt: A DAG has vertices A,B,C,D and edges A→C, B→C, C→D. In the order B,A,C,D, how many directed edges point backward in the order?
questions.explanation: B and A both precede C, and C precedes D. Every edge points forward, so the ordering is topological and has zero backward edges.

questions.prompt: Kahn's topological-sort algorithm repeatedly removes a vertex of what current property?
options: Indegree zero
Maximum outdegree
Smallest DFS finish time
Largest edge weight
answer: Indegree zero
questions.explanation: A vertex with current indegree zero has no remaining prerequisite. Removing it and decrementing successor indegrees constructs a topological ordering.

questions.prompt: What can be concluded if Kahn's algorithm removes fewer vertices than the DAG input contains?
options: The directed graph contains a cycle
Some vertices remain in a cyclic dependency region or depend on it
The graph must be undirected
A topological ordering was completed
answer: The directed graph contains a cycle
Some vertices remain in a cyclic dependency region or depend on it
questions.explanation: If vertices remain, each has positive residual indegree. Following incoming dependencies in a finite directed graph eventually reveals a cycle; downstream vertices may also remain blocked.

questions.prompt: A DAG's vertices are ordered by decreasing DFS finish time. What does this order provide?
options: A topological ordering
A minimum spanning tree
An Euler circuit
A shortest-path tree for arbitrary weights
answer: A topological ordering
questions.explanation: For a DAG, every edge u→v has finish time of u greater than finish time of v. Sorting by decreasing finish time therefore places u before v.

questions.prompt: A simple undirected graph has 8 vertices and is complete. How many edges does it contain?
questions.explanation: A complete simple undirected graph has V(V−1)/2 edges. For V=8, this is 8×7/2=28.

questions.prompt: Which statements about graph representations are correct?
options: An adjacency matrix uses Θ(V²) space
An adjacency list uses Θ(V+E) space
Testing whether an edge exists is O(1) in an adjacency matrix
Iterating neighbors is usually efficient with adjacency lists
answer: An adjacency matrix uses Θ(V²) space
An adjacency list uses Θ(V+E) space
Testing whether an edge exists is O(1) in an adjacency matrix
Iterating neighbors is usually efficient with adjacency lists
questions.explanation: Matrices allocate one cell per vertex pair and allow constant-time edge lookup. Lists store vertices and incident edges, making neighbor iteration efficient for sparse graphs.

questions.prompt: For a sparse graph with E=O(V), which representation usually uses asymptotically less space?
options: Adjacency list
Adjacency matrix
Both use Θ(V²)
Neither can represent it
answer: Adjacency list
questions.explanation: An adjacency list uses Θ(V+E)=Θ(V) space for a sparse graph. An adjacency matrix always uses Θ(V²) space.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has 9 vertices and every vertex has degree 4. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: By the handshaking lemma, the degree sum is 2E. Here 9×4=36=2E, so E=18.

questions.prompt: In an unweighted graph, BFS from s discovers v at level 5. What is the distance from s to v?
options: 5 edges
5 vertices total
At least 10 edges
It cannot be known
answer: 5 edges
questions.explanation: BFS level records the number of edges in a shortest path from the source. A vertex discovered at level five has distance five.

questions.prompt: Which statements about BFS and DFS differ in general?
options: BFS uses a queue and explores by distance layers
DFS uses a stack-like discipline and explores deeply
BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs
DFS always has lower time complexity than BFS
answer: BFS uses a queue and explores by distance layers
DFS uses a stack-like discipline and explores deeply
BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs
questions.explanation: Both traversals take O(V+E) on adjacency lists. Their frontier discipline differs, and only BFS provides shortest paths by edge count in general unweighted graphs.

questions.prompt: A BFS queue begins with source s. The graph has edges s–a, s–b, a–c, b–d, and c–e. What is the shortest-path distance from s to e?
questions.explanation: A path s–a–c–e has three edges. BFS layers are s at 0, a and b at 1, c and d at 2, and e at 3.

questions.prompt: A directed graph is strongly connected when which condition holds?
options: Every vertex can reach every other vertex
It has exactly one source vertex
Its underlying undirected graph is a tree
Every vertex has equal indegree and outdegree
answer: Every vertex can reach every other vertex
questions.explanation: Strong connectivity requires directed paths in both directions between every pair of vertices.

questions.prompt: Which statements about strongly connected components (SCCs) are correct?
options: Each SCC is a maximal strongly connected vertex set
Contracting each SCC produces a DAG
Kosaraju's algorithm uses DFS on the graph and its transpose
Every graph has exactly one SCC
answer: Each SCC is a maximal strongly connected vertex set
Contracting each SCC produces a DAG
Kosaraju's algorithm uses DFS on the graph and its transpose
questions.explanation: SCCs partition directed vertices into maximal mutually reachable sets. The condensation graph is acyclic, and Kosaraju uses finishing order plus a traversal of the transpose.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has 10 vertices partitioned into 4 strongly connected components. How many vertices belong to each component on average?
questions.explanation: The mean component size is total vertices divided by component count: 10/4=2.5.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm finds a minimum spanning tree by sorting edges and maintaining components?
options: Kruskal's algorithm
BFS
Dijkstra's algorithm
Topological sorting
answer: Kruskal's algorithm
questions.explanation: Kruskal sorts edges by weight and adds edges connecting distinct components, commonly using disjoint-set union.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 6 vertices. How many edges does any spanning tree contain?
questions.explanation: A tree on V vertices has V−1 edges. For six vertices, the spanning tree has five edges.

questions.prompt: Which statements about minimum spanning trees are correct?
options: An MST is defined for a connected undirected weighted graph
It minimizes the sum of selected edge weights
It contains V−1 edges
It necessarily gives shortest paths from a chosen source
answer: An MST is defined for a connected undirected weighted graph
It minimizes the sum of selected edge weights
It contains V−1 edges
questions.explanation: An MST minimizes total tree weight and has V−1 edges. It does not necessarily preserve shortest paths from a source; that is a different optimization objective.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm is applied to a graph with edge weights 2, 5, and 1. If the current distance to u is 7 and edge u→v has weight 5, what candidate distance is relaxed for v?
questions.explanation: Relaxation considers d(u)+w(u,v)=7+5=12 as a candidate distance for v.

questions.prompt: A directed path has edge weights 4, 2, and 7. What is its total path weight?
questions.explanation: Path weights add along the edges: 4+2+7=13.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Dijkstra's algorithm are correct?
options: It works with nonnegative edge weights
It can be implemented with a priority queue
It is generally incorrect with negative edges
It computes all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³) by definition
answer: It works with nonnegative edge weights
It can be implemented with a priority queue
It is generally incorrect with negative edges
questions.explanation: Dijkstra is a single-source method relying on nonnegative weights. A priority queue supports minimum tentative-distance extraction; Floyd–Warshall is a standard all-pairs DP algorithm.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm can find shortest paths when negative edge weights exist, provided there is no reachable negative cycle?
options: Bellman-Ford
Dijkstra
Prim
BFS
answer: Bellman-Ford
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford repeatedly relaxes all edges and supports negative weights. It can also detect a reachable negative cycle after V−1 passes.

questions.prompt: A graph has V=7 vertices. How many full edge-relaxation passes does Bellman-Ford perform before its negative-cycle check?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford needs at most V−1 passes to propagate shortest paths with at most V−1 edges. For seven vertices, this is six passes.

questions.prompt: Which conditions indicate a reachable negative cycle in Bellman-Ford analysis?
options: After V−1 passes, some edge can still be relaxed
There is a path from the source to the cycle
Every edge weight is negative
A shortest path value is finite and stable
answer: After V−1 passes, some edge can still be relaxed
There is a path from the source to the cycle
questions.explanation: A reachable negative cycle permits arbitrarily decreasing path costs. After V−1 passes, a further possible relaxation signals such a cycle; an unreachable negative cycle does not affect source distances.

questions.prompt: Floyd–Warshall updates distance d[i,j] through intermediate vertex k. Which recurrence is used?
options: d[i,j]=min(d[i,j], d[i,k]+d[k,j])
d[i,j]=max(d[i,k], d[k,j])
d[i,j]=d[i,k]×d[k,j]
d[i,j]=d[i,j]+1
answer: d[i,j]=min(d[i,j], d[i,k]+d[k,j])
questions.explanation: For each permitted intermediate k, the algorithm compares the existing route with a route from i to k followed by k to j.

questions.prompt: Floyd–Warshall is run on a graph with 5 vertices. How many intermediate-vertex iterations are performed?
questions.explanation: The algorithm considers each vertex as an allowed intermediate exactly once, so there are five outer iterations.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Floyd–Warshall are correct?
options: Its time complexity is O(V³)
It computes all-pairs shortest paths
It can handle negative edges if there is no negative cycle
It uses a greedy frontier expansion from one source
answer: Its time complexity is O(V³)
It computes all-pairs shortest paths
It can handle negative edges if there is no negative cycle
questions.explanation: Floyd–Warshall is a triple-loop dynamic program for all pairs and allows negative edges absent negative cycles. It is not a single-source greedy algorithm.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has an edge u→v with weight −3 and a reachable negative cycle. What happens to the shortest-path distance for vertices reachable from that cycle?
options: No finite minimum distance exists for affected vertices
The distance is always zero
Dijkstra returns the correct finite distance
The cycle can be ignored
answer: No finite minimum distance exists for affected vertices
questions.explanation: Traversing a reachable negative cycle repeatedly decreases path cost without bound. For vertices reachable from it, a finite shortest-path value is undefined.

questions.prompt: An unweighted graph has a shortest path of 7 edges from s to t. What is the BFS distance label assigned to t?
questions.explanation: BFS distance is measured by the number of edges in a shortest path. Therefore t receives label seven.

questions.prompt: Which statements about DFS edge classification in a directed graph are correct?
options: A back edge points to an ancestor in the DFS forest
A forward edge points to a descendant but is not a tree edge
A cross edge connects vertices with no ancestor-descendant relation
A back edge proves the graph is acyclic
answer: A back edge points to an ancestor in the DFS forest
A forward edge points to a descendant but is not a tree edge
A cross edge connects vertices with no ancestor-descendant relation
questions.explanation: These categories use discovery/finish nesting in the DFS forest. Back edges indicate a directed cycle, while forward and cross edges have different ancestor relationships.

questions.prompt: In a DAG, DFS finishes vertex u after all vertices reachable from u have finished. What does decreasing finish-time order ensure for every edge u→v?
options: u appears before v
v appears before u
u and v are adjacent in the order
The edge is removed
answer: u appears before v
questions.explanation: For a DAG there are no back edges, and every edge leads to a vertex that finishes earlier. Decreasing finish times therefore place u before v.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has 10 vertices and 3 connected components. How many edges does a spanning forest contain if each component is connected internally?
questions.explanation: A spanning forest with c components and V vertices has V−c edges. Here 10−3=7.

questions.prompt: Which statements about connected components in an undirected graph are correct?
options: A DFS from one unvisited vertex reaches every vertex in its component
Starting DFS again from each unvisited vertex enumerates components
Every connected component has a spanning tree
A disconnected graph has exactly one component
answer: A DFS from one unvisited vertex reaches every vertex in its component
Starting DFS again from each unvisited vertex enumerates components
Every connected component has a spanning tree
questions.explanation: Traversal follows all reachable vertices, and repeating from unvisited vertices yields each component. A disconnected graph has at least two components.

questions.prompt: A topological ordering of a DAG is not unique. What does this indicate?
options: At least one pair of currently incomparable vertices can appear in different valid orders
The graph contains a cycle
The graph is disconnected
Every edge has the same weight
answer: At least one pair of currently incomparable vertices can appear in different valid orders
questions.explanation: If multiple topological orders exist, some vertices have no precedence constraint forcing one fixed relative order. A cycle would make every topological order impossible.

questions.prompt: A directed acyclic graph has 6 vertices and a topological order. How many edges can point from a later vertex to an earlier vertex in that order?
questions.explanation: By definition, every directed edge must point forward in a topological order. Therefore no edge points backward.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has an odd cycle. Which property is impossible?
options: Being bipartite
Being connected
Having a spanning tree
Having a DFS traversal
answer: Being bipartite
questions.explanation: A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle. An odd cycle cannot be colored with two colors without adjacent equal colors.

questions.prompt: Which methods can test whether an undirected graph is bipartite?
options: Two-color vertices using BFS
Two-color vertices using DFS
Detect an odd cycle
Run topological sorting
answer: Two-color vertices using BFS
Two-color vertices using DFS
Detect an odd cycle
questions.explanation: BFS or DFS can assign alternating colors and detect a conflict. The equivalent structural characterization is the absence of odd cycles; topological sorting applies to directed acyclic graphs.

questions.prompt: A bipartite graph coloring assigns color 0 to s. Every neighbor is assigned color 1. If a vertex is reached by a path of 6 edges from s, what color does it receive?
questions.explanation: Colors alternate at each edge. An even-length path returns to the source color, so after six edges the color is 0.

questions.prompt: A graph contains a self-loop. Which conclusion follows?
options: It is not bipartite
It is necessarily a tree
It has no cycles
It must be disconnected
answer: It is not bipartite
questions.explanation: A self-loop is an odd cycle of length one and requires its endpoint to have a different color from itself, which is impossible in a bipartite graph.

questions.prompt: Which statements about shortest paths in unweighted graphs are correct?
options: BFS gives a shortest path by edge count
DFS discovery order need not give a shortest path
A shortest path can be reconstructed using parent pointers
All shortest paths between a pair must be unique
answer: BFS gives a shortest path by edge count
DFS discovery order need not give a shortest path
A shortest path can be reconstructed using parent pointers
questions.explanation: BFS distances are optimal by layers, and parent pointers record one shortest path. Multiple distinct paths of the same minimum length may exist.

questions.prompt: An undirected tree has 20 vertices. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Every tree has one fewer edge than vertices, so 20−1=19.

questions.prompt: For a graph stored as an adjacency matrix, what is the time to scan all possible neighbors of one vertex?
options: Θ(V)
Θ(E)
Θ(log V)
answer: Θ(V)
questions.explanation: The matrix row has one entry for every possible destination vertex. Scanning that row takes Θ(V) time regardless of the actual degree.

questions.prompt: Which statements about graph traversal complexity are correct?
options: Adjacency-list BFS is O(V+E)
Adjacency-matrix BFS is O(V²)
A traversal of a disconnected graph must start from every component to visit all vertices
BFS and DFS have different asymptotic complexity on the same representation
answer: Adjacency-list BFS is O(V+E)
Adjacency-matrix BFS is O(V²)
A traversal of a disconnected graph must start from every component to visit all vertices
questions.explanation: Adjacency lists scan actual edges; matrices scan all possible neighbors. BFS and DFS have the same asymptotic traversal cost for a fixed representation.

questions.prompt: A simple undirected graph has 15 edges. What is the sum of all vertex degrees?
questions.explanation: The handshaking lemma states that the sum of degrees equals 2E. For 15 edges, the sum is 30.

questions.prompt: A connected undirected graph has exactly V−1 edges. What can be concluded?
options: It is a tree
It must contain a cycle
It is complete
It is directed
answer: It is a tree
questions.explanation: A connected graph with V vertices and V−1 edges is acyclic and therefore a tree. Equivalently, it has the minimum number of edges needed for connectivity.

questions.prompt: Which facts about a tree are correct?
options: There is exactly one simple path between any two vertices
A tree with V vertices has V−1 edges
Removing any edge disconnects a tree
Adding any new edge creates a cycle
answer: There is exactly one simple path between any two vertices
A tree with V vertices has V−1 edges
Removing any edge disconnects a tree
Adding any new edge creates a cycle
questions.explanation: These are equivalent structural properties of trees. A tree is connected and acyclic; removing an edge breaks connectivity, while an added edge closes the unique existing path into a cycle.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has 7 vertices and is a DAG. How many edges must be reversed in a valid topological order?
questions.explanation: A topological ordering already places every edge's tail before its head. Thus no edge needs to be reversed.

questions.prompt: A graph has negative edge weights but no negative cycles. Which shortest-path method is appropriate for all-pairs distances?
options: Floyd–Warshall
BFS
Prim
Kruskal
answer: Floyd–Warshall
questions.explanation: Floyd–Warshall handles negative edges and computes all-pairs shortest paths, provided no negative cycle makes distances unbounded below.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the Bellman–Ford algorithm are correct?
options: Its standard time is O(VE)
It supports negative edge weights
It can detect a reachable negative cycle
It finalizes the closest unsettled vertex each iteration
answer: Its standard time is O(VE)
It supports negative edge weights
It can detect a reachable negative cycle
questions.explanation: Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges for V−1 rounds and checks for further improvement. The closest-unsettled greedy rule describes Dijkstra, not Bellman–Ford.

questions.prompt: Bellman–Ford is run on a graph with 9 vertices and 20 edges. What is the asymptotic number of edge relaxations in its main V−1 passes?
questions.explanation: There are 8 passes over 20 edges, giving 8×20=160 relaxation attempts, excluding the final cycle-detection pass.

questions.prompt: Floyd–Warshall's triple loop has one iteration for each ordered pair (i,j) and each intermediate k. What is its time complexity?
options: Θ(V³)
Θ(V²)
Θ(E log V)
Θ(VE)
answer: Θ(V³)
questions.explanation: There are V choices for i, V for j, and V for k, giving V³ constant-time updates.

questions.prompt: Which statements about shortest-path algorithms are correct?
options: BFS is suitable for unweighted edges
Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights
Bellman–Ford can handle negative edges
Prim minimizes source-to-vertex distances
answer: BFS is suitable for unweighted edges
Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights
Bellman–Ford can handle negative edges
questions.explanation: BFS optimizes hop count, Dijkstra handles nonnegative weighted paths, and Bellman–Ford permits negative weights. Prim optimizes total spanning-tree weight, not source distances.

questions.prompt: In a weighted graph, a path uses edges with weights 3, 8, and 2. What is its total weight?
questions.explanation: Add the weights along the path: 3+8+2=13.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has a negative cycle that is not reachable from source s. Does it invalidate Bellman–Ford distances from s?
options: No, only reachable negative cycles affect source distances
Yes, every negative cycle affects every source
It makes all distances zero
It converts the graph into an undirected graph
answer: No, only reachable negative cycles affect source distances
questions.explanation: A source-based shortest path can use only vertices reachable from that source. An unreachable negative cycle cannot be traversed from s and does not affect its distances.

questions.prompt: Which statements about topological sorting are correct?
options: A DAG may have multiple valid topological orders
A topological order can be found in O(V+E)
Every edge u→v requires u before v
A topological order exists for every directed graph
answer: A DAG may have multiple valid topological orders
A topological order can be found in O(V+E)
Every edge u→v requires u before v
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm or DFS computes an order in linear graph time. The order is not necessarily unique, and cycles make it impossible.

questions.prompt: A DAG has 8 vertices and 10 edges. How many total indegree decrements does Kahn's algorithm perform when all vertices are removed?
questions.explanation: Each directed edge contributes one to a destination's indegree and is processed once when its source is removed. Thus there are 10 decrements.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has a BFS tree rooted at s. What do tree edges guarantee about endpoint levels?
options: Their levels differ by exactly one
Their levels are always equal
Their weights are equal
They are all bridges
answer: Their levels differ by exactly one
questions.explanation: A BFS tree edge connects a vertex to the parent that discovered it, so the child's level is exactly one more than the parent's.

questions.prompt: Which statements about DFS discovery and finishing times are correct?
options: A vertex's discovery time precedes its finishing time
Ancestor intervals are nested
They can support topological sorting of a DAG
They directly give shortest-path distances in an unweighted graph
answer: A vertex's discovery time precedes its finishing time
Ancestor intervals are nested
They can support topological sorting of a DAG
questions.explanation: DFS timestamps create nested intervals for ancestor relationships and decreasing finish times yield a topological order in a DAG. They do not replace BFS distance layers.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 11 vertices. How many edges are in its DFS spanning tree?
questions.explanation: A DFS spanning tree on 11 connected vertices contains 11−1=10 tree edges.

questions.prompt: A graph's adjacency list has total degree sum 40 and is undirected. How many edges does it contain?
questions.explanation: Each undirected edge appears in the adjacency lists of both endpoints, so the degree sum is 2E. Hence E=40/2=20.

questions.prompt: Which statements about undirected graph edge counts are correct for a simple graph?
options: A vertex has degree at most V−1
The complete graph has V(V−1)/2 edges
The sum of all degrees is 2E
A self-loop contributes one to the degree sum
answer: A vertex has degree at most V−1
The complete graph has V(V−1)/2 edges
The sum of all degrees is 2E
questions.explanation: A simple graph has no self-loops or parallel edges. Every edge contributes one degree to each endpoint, yielding 2E; loops are excluded by simplicity.

questions.prompt: A complete graph on 10 vertices has how many edges?
questions.explanation: The number of unordered vertex pairs is 10×9/2=45, one edge per pair.

questions.prompt: A graph has V vertices and E edges. A disjoint-set structure used by Kruskal performs which central operation?
options: Determine whether two vertices currently belong to the same component
Find a shortest path between two vertices
Order vertices by BFS level
Compute all-pairs distances
answer: Determine whether two vertices currently belong to the same component
questions.explanation: Find operations compare component representatives; union merges components after accepting an edge. This prevents cycles during Kruskal's MST construction.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Kruskal's algorithm are correct?
options: It sorts edges by nondecreasing weight
It maintains a forest of selected edges
It rejects an edge if both endpoints already share a component
It requires edge weights to be positive
answer: It sorts edges by nondecreasing weight
It maintains a forest of selected edges
It rejects an edge if both endpoints already share a component
questions.explanation: Kruskal needs weight order and cycle avoidance; negative weights are allowed. The forest components are maintained using disjoint-set union.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 8 vertices and its MST contains edge weights 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. What is the total MST weight?
questions.explanation: The tree contains seven edges. Their weights sum to 1+2+3+4+5+6+7=28.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes an MST from a shortest-path tree?
options: An MST minimizes total tree-edge weight, while a shortest-path tree preserves distances from a source
An MST is always a shortest-path tree
A shortest-path tree must include every graph edge
Both optimize the same objective
answer: An MST minimizes total tree-edge weight, while a shortest-path tree preserves distances from a source
questions.explanation: The objectives differ: MST optimizes the sum over selected edges, while a shortest-path tree preserves distances from one chosen source. They can produce different trees.

questions.prompt: Which conditions make an edge safe to include in some minimum spanning tree under the cut property?
options: It is a lightest edge crossing a cut
It has the largest weight in the graph
It lies entirely within one side of every cut
A unique lightest crossing edge is mandatory in every MST
answer: It is a lightest edge crossing a cut
A unique lightest crossing edge is mandatory in every MST
questions.explanation: Any light edge crossing a cut is safe for some MST; if it is uniquely lightest across that cut, every MST must include it.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 20 vertices. How many edges are in any spanning tree?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree contains V−1 edges. For 20 vertices that is 19.

questions.prompt: In a directed acyclic graph, which method can compute longest path distances in linear time after topological sorting?
options: Relax edges in topological order
Run Dijkstra with negative weights
Use Kruskal's algorithm
Perform BFS from every vertex only
answer: Relax edges in topological order
questions.explanation: A topological order ensures every predecessor is processed before a vertex. Relaxing outgoing edges once in that order computes DAG longest-path values in O(V+E), even with negative weights.

questions.prompt: Which statements about shortest paths in a DAG are correct?
options: They can be computed by edge relaxation in topological order
Negative edge weights are allowed
A DAG has no negative cycle
The algorithm requires a nonnegative-weight condition like Dijkstra
answer: They can be computed by edge relaxation in topological order
Negative edge weights are allowed
A DAG has no negative cycle
questions.explanation: A DAG's topological order permits each edge to be relaxed once, handling negative weights safely because cycles do not exist. Dijkstra's nonnegative restriction is not needed.

questions.prompt: A DAG has vertices s,a,b,t and edges s→a weight 2, s→b weight 5, a→t weight 7, b→t weight 1. What is the shortest distance from s to t?
questions.explanation: The path through a costs 2+7=9, while the path through b costs 5+1=6. The shortest distance is 6.

questions.prompt: A graph is represented by an adjacency matrix. What is the space complexity even if it has only O(V) edges?
options: Θ(V²)
Θ(V+E)
Θ(E log V)
Θ(V)
answer: Θ(V²)
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix allocates a cell for every ordered or unordered vertex pair, so space remains quadratic independent of sparsity.

questions.prompt: Which statements about BFS parent pointers are correct?
options: They define a shortest-path tree for reachable vertices
Following parents from a vertex reaches the source
A vertex's parent is always its numerically smallest neighbor
Unreachable vertices have no BFS parent from the source
answer: They define a shortest-path tree for reachable vertices
Following parents from a vertex reaches the source
Unreachable vertices have no BFS parent from the source
questions.explanation: Each parent is the vertex that first discovered a node, so parent chains form shortest paths back to the source. An unreachable vertex is never assigned a parent by that BFS.

questions.prompt: A BFS tree has source level 0 and a vertex at level 6. How many parent edges are followed from that vertex back to the source?
questions.explanation: Each parent step decreases the level by one. A level-6 vertex therefore follows six tree edges to reach level zero.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has no directed cycles. Which statement about its SCCs is necessarily true?
options: Every SCC contains exactly one vertex
All vertices belong to one SCC
There are no SCCs
Each SCC must contain a directed cycle
answer: Every SCC contains exactly one vertex
questions.explanation: Without directed cycles, no two distinct vertices can reach each other in both directions. Each vertex is therefore its own strongly connected component.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the condensation graph of SCCs are correct?
options: Each SCC becomes one vertex
Edges between components preserve intercomponent reachability
The condensation graph is a DAG
It must be strongly connected
answer: Each SCC becomes one vertex
Edges between components preserve intercomponent reachability
The condensation graph is a DAG
questions.explanation: Contracting mutually reachable sets removes all directed cycles between components; otherwise those components would form one larger SCC. The resulting condensation graph is acyclic.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has 5 vertices. Floyd–Warshall initializes d[i,i] to what value when there is no negative cycle?
questions.explanation: The empty path from a vertex to itself has weight zero, so the diagonal of the initial distance matrix is zero.

questions.prompt: A weighted graph has two routes from s to t: one with weights 4 and 8, another with weights 5, 2, and 3. What is the shortest route weight?
questions.explanation: The first path costs 4+8=12. The second costs 5+2+3=10, so the minimum is 10.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the relaxation operation are correct?
options: It replaces d[v] if d[u]+w(u,v) is smaller
It can improve a tentative distance
Repeated relaxation is central to Bellman–Ford
It is valid only for undirected graphs
answer: It replaces d[v] if d[u]+w(u,v) is smaller
It can improve a tentative distance
Repeated relaxation is central to Bellman–Ford
questions.explanation: Relaxation checks whether a path through u improves the known estimate for v. It applies to directed or undirected edge representations and is fundamental to several shortest-path algorithms.

questions.prompt: A BFS is run from s in an unweighted graph. If v is first discovered from u, what is the relationship between their distances?
options: dist[v]=dist[u]+1
dist[v]=dist[u]
dist[v]=2dist[u]
No relationship is guaranteed
answer: dist[v]=dist[u]+1
questions.explanation: Every BFS tree edge connects consecutive layers. A newly discovered neighbor receives distance one greater than its discovering vertex.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has degrees 1, 2, 2, 3, and 4. How many edges are present?
questions.explanation: The degree sum is 1+2+2+3+4=12. By the handshaking lemma, the edge count is 12/2=6.

questions.prompt: Which statements about graph cycles and trees are correct?
options: A connected acyclic undirected graph is a tree
A connected graph with V−1 edges is a tree
Every undirected graph has a spanning tree
A cycle has at least one edge whose removal preserves connectivity of that cycle's vertices
answer: A connected acyclic undirected graph is a tree
A connected graph with V−1 edges is a tree
A cycle has at least one edge whose removal preserves connectivity of that cycle's vertices
questions.explanation: Connectedness plus acyclicity characterizes trees, as does connectedness with V−1 edges. Removing one edge from a cycle leaves an alternate path between its endpoints; disconnected graphs do not have a spanning tree over all vertices.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is appropriate for all-pairs shortest paths in a dense graph with moderate V?
options: Floyd–Warshall
BFS from one source only
Prim
Kruskal
answer: Floyd–Warshall
questions.explanation: Floyd–Warshall computes distances for every ordered vertex pair in O(V³) time and O(V²) space, making it suitable for moderate dense graphs.

questions.prompt: An adjacency matrix for a graph with 40 vertices has how many entries?
questions.explanation: A square adjacency matrix has V² entries, so 40²=1600 cells.

questions.prompt: Which statements about BFS on a disconnected undirected graph are correct?
options: A BFS from one source visits only its connected component
A BFS forest can be built by starting from each unvisited vertex
Every component receives a separate tree in a full traversal
A single BFS necessarily reaches all vertices
answer: A BFS from one source visits only its connected component
A BFS forest can be built by starting from each unvisited vertex
Every component receives a separate tree in a full traversal
questions.explanation: Reachability limits a single BFS to one component. Repeating from each unvisited vertex creates a BFS forest with one tree per component.

questions.prompt: A graph has a unique lightest edge crossing a particular cut. Which MST principle applies?
options: The cut property requires this edge in every MST
The cycle property excludes the edge
The edge cannot be part of any spanning tree
The edge is relevant only to shortest paths
answer: The cut property requires this edge in every MST
questions.explanation: The unique minimum-weight edge crossing a cut is safe and belongs to every minimum spanning tree.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has 6 vertices, each with exactly one outgoing edge. What is the total number of directed edges?
questions.explanation: Summing the outdegrees gives the number of directed edges. Six vertices each contribute one outgoing edge, totaling six.

questions.prompt: Which algorithmic facts are true for a DAG?
options: It admits a topological ordering
It contains no directed cycle
Shortest paths can be computed by topological edge relaxation even with negative weights
Dijkstra is always necessary for its shortest paths
answer: It admits a topological ordering
It contains no directed cycle
Shortest paths can be computed by topological edge relaxation even with negative weights
questions.explanation: A DAG is exactly a directed graph with a topological ordering. Relaxing edges in that order computes shortest paths in linear time and supports negative edges; Dijkstra is unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A BFS tree contains a vertex at level 0, four vertices at level 1, and six vertices at level 2. How many vertices are in these explored levels?
questions.explanation: Count the disjoint BFS layers: 1+4+6=11 vertices have been discovered through level two.

questions.prompt: Kahn's algorithm processes a DAG by repeatedly removing a zero-indegree vertex. Which condition guarantees that the DAG has a unique topological ordering?
answer: At every step there is exactly one zero-indegree vertex among the remaining vertices
questions.explanation: A topological order is unique precisely when Kahn's process has no choice at any step. Multiple available zero-indegree vertices can be selected in different orders.
options: Every vertex has outdegree at most one
At every step there is exactly one zero-indegree vertex among the remaining vertices
The graph has exactly one source initially
Every directed path has the same length

questions.prompt: A graph has negative edge weights but no negative cycles. Which algorithm can compute single-source shortest paths in O(VE) time?
options: Bellman–Ford
Dijkstra
BFS
Prim
answer: Bellman–Ford
questions.explanation: Bellman–Ford performs up to V−1 passes over all edges and supports negative weights. It detects reachable negative cycles with an additional pass.
